en: The Sūtra on the Self-Transformation of the Buddha for Ajita Keśakambalin Concerning Suffering;
Translator Unknown.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vulture Peak Mountain in Rājagṛha. At that time,
In the early morning, the World-Honored One dressed himself, took up his bowl, and departed from Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain to enter the city of Rājagṛha for alms.
At that time, Ajita Keśakambalin, having some minor business to attend to, was leaving the city of Rājagṛha and heading toward Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain.
Seeing the World-Honored One from afar, he approached the Buddha and addressed him, saying:
"Gautama! I wish to ask a question; would you have the leisure to grant me an answer?"
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"This is not the time for discussion. I am now entering the city to beg for alms; when I have returned, that will be the time, and I shall speak for you."
The second time he spoke likewise, and the third time he asked again: "Gautama,
why do you create obstacles for me?"
"Gautama! In what way is there a difference?
I now wish to ask a question; please explain it to me."
The Buddha said to Ajita Kesakambalin,
"Ask whatever you wish.
Ajita Kesakambalin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How is it, Gautama— is suffering created by oneself?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"That 'suffering is self-made' is an indeterminate [teaching].
Kāśyapa asked again: "How so, Gautama?"
“Is suffering created by another?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
“That suffering is created by another is also indeterminate.”
Kāśyapa asked again:
"Is suffering created by oneself or by another?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Suffering is created by both self and others;
this too is undeclared. Kāśyapa asked again: "How so, Gautama?"
“Is suffering neither self-made nor made by another, but produced without cause?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
“That suffering is neither self-made nor made by another, but produced without cause—this too is undeclared.”
Kāśyapa asked again: "Gautama! Regarding what was asked:
is suffering created by oneself?"
He replied, "It is indeterminate. [The interlocutor asked:
"Is it created by another?
Or is it created by both self and another?"
"Is it not created by oneself, nor by another, nor produced without cause?
He replied, "It is indeterminate.
"In that case, does this suffering not exist now?"
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"It is not that this suffering does not exist; rather, this suffering does exist.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Excellent, Gautama!
You have declared that this suffering exists; please teach me the Dharma so that I may know suffering and see suffering.”
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"If that which experiences were itself the experiencer, I would say that suffering is self-created;
if that which is experienced by another were itself the experiencer, then it would be created by another."
If suffering were experienced by oneself, or if it were experienced by another and then inflicted upon oneself, I would say that it is produced by both self and other;
nor do I say that suffering arises without cause, being neither dependent on self nor on another.
Departing from these extremes, he taught the Middle Way:
"When this exists, that exists; with the arising of this, that arises.

That is to say, conditioned by ignorance, there are volitional formations, and so on, until the entire great mass of suffering arises. With the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease, and so on, until the entire great mass of suffering ceases.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, Ajita Keśakambalin was distanced from dust and freed from defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye.

At that time, having seen the Dharma, attained the Dharma, known the Dharma, and entered the Dharma, he crossed over all doubts; no longer relying on others for knowledge and not being delivered by others, his mind attained fearlessness regarding the True Dharma and Vinaya. Joining his palms, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!...”

I have now crossed over; from this day forth, I take refuge in the Buddha, I take refuge in the Dharma, and I take refuge in the Sangha. For as long as life lasts, may you bear witness that I am an upāsaka.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, Ajita Kesakambalin rejoiced and delighted in it; he paid homage and departed.

Not long after Ajita Kesakambalin had left the World-Honored One, he was gored to death by a cow that was protecting her calf. At the moment of his death, his faculties were pure and his complexion was bright and clear.
At that time, the World-Honored One entered the city to beg for food.

There were also many bhikṣus who had entered the city of Rājagṛha to beg for food; they heard a report that Aciravata Kāśyapa, having heard the Dharma from the World-Honored One, had departed not long ago when he was gored to death by an ox. At the moment of his death, his faculties were pure and his complexion was bright and white.

Having finished their almsround and returned from it, the bhikṣus put away their robes and bowls, washed their feet, went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to sit on one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

This morning, while many bhikṣus and I were entering the city for alms, we heard that Aciravata Kāśyapa, having heard the Dharma and Vinaya from the World-Honored One, had departed not long ago and was struck and killed by a cow protecting its calf; at the moment of his death, his faculties were pure and his complexion was bright and clear.
"Bhagavān! To which realm of existence was he born?
In what place did he take birth?"
"What has he attained?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"He has seen the Dharma and known the Dharma; having lived in accordance with the Dharma, he did not grasp at any phenomena and has entered parinirvāṇa. You should go and make offerings to his body."
At that time, the World-Honored One bestowed the first prediction upon Acelakāśyapa.
This concludes the *Buddha’s Discourse on Acelakāśyapa Transforming Himself to Manifest Suffering*, in one fascicle.
